content.thinking:
I need to be careful with the postmortem facts, using figure names rather than writing numbers myself. Looking at the timeline, there's a discrepancy: the deploy happened at 10:35, but the flag-toggle log shows a split between off and on states at that same moment, which doesn't match the recorded toggle time of 10:40:17 — I need to flag this inconsistency.

The errors (ZeroDivisionError) ran from 10:35 to 10:40, and recovery came at 10:42 after the flag was reverted at 10:41:31, confirming the flag revert as the fix even though the underlying code defect (dividing by purchase count with no zero-guard) remains unaddressed in a draft PR. I'll note the timing ambiguity between when logs show the flag evaluating "on" versus the recorded toggle event as an unresolved discrepancy rather than trying to reconcile it myself.

Continuing why it shipped: no test for empty-month accounts, the flag ramp wasn't gated, rollback was unreachable, and the alert lagged about 5m46s behind onset — that gap itself needs an action item, citing M1/T19 for the rollback issue and the flag revert (T22, T24) stopping errors. For action items, I'm separating the actual fix (AI-2) from a new test guarding zero-purchase accounts (AI-3) and a detection improvement for the alert lag.

For remediation, I'm adding a rollback fallback when the platform is unreachable, tying flag ramps to deploys with staged error-rate monitoring, and reconciling the flag audit timestamp mismatch — each contributing factor needs to map to one of these.

For lessons, I'm noting the lucky save (the flag lever existing despite the platform being unreachable, though the underlying defect remains so re-enabling the flag would retrigger it), what went well (Argus's fast fallback and confirmed recovery), and what went wrong (the investigator underranking the flag fix, the unreachable rollback, and the slow alert). I'm being careful to avoid writing specific numbers, timestamps, or identifiers like PR numbers in the final write-up, using descriptive names instead, and now drafting the executive summary using the duration and error-count placeholders.

action_items.item: Add a regression test for the spend summary covering accounts the failing division cannot handle, and make the code handle that case explicitly instead of dividing. Run it in CI for the proposed fix.

Add a faster alert on the account-page error rate, using a short window and a lower threshold. It should page closer to the start of a deploy-correlated rise, to cut the gap between {began} and {alert_raised}.

Require staged exposure for flags that gate newly deployed code. Ramp in steps with an error-rate check between steps, and do not enable a flag in the same window as the deploy that introduces its code. Also reconcile the flag-change audit timestamps with the evaluation logs.
Give rollbacks a fallback when the deployment platform is unreachable, such as an alternate access path. Add a health check on Argus's reach to the platform so the gap is found before an incident.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account-page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, between {began} and {recovered}. The alert fired at {alert_raised}.

The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py line 47. It occurred {G5309.1} times over the window, and the earlier baseline errors were unrelated client disconnects.
That code arrived with the revision deployed at {began}, the same minute the errors began. The spend-summary arithmetic fails for some accounts, so any request that reaches it can throw.

The flag monthly-spend-feature decided how much traffic reached that code. Before the deploy every evaluation was off. From {began}, evaluations were mixed, with {G971b.2} off and {G971b.3} on, and later every evaluation was on. The flag change event is stamped later than the log shows, so the exact moment it took effect is uncertain.

Nothing stopped the defect before it reached shoppers. The release and the flag exposure landed together without a guard against the failing case. The platform rollback was unavailable. Reverting the flag removed the traffic from the faulty path, and the service was back at baseline from {recovered}, while the defective code stayed deployed.

contributing_factors.factor: The new spend-summary code reached production without a test or guard for accounts that trigger the division by zero, so the defect was only found by live traffic.

The release and the flag ramp-up happened together, with no staged exposure and no error-rate check between steps. The flag change record also disagrees with the flag evaluations in the logs, which makes the sequence hard to reconstruct.
The alert fired well after the errors began, a gap of {alert_raised - began}, so shoppers were affected before anyone was paged.
The deployment platform was unreachable, so the rollback Argus tried first could not run. Recovery depended on the flag being available as a second lever.
The defective code is still deployed behind the flag, so re-enabling the flag would bring the outage back until the fix merges.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a share of account-page requests on the io-shop storefront failed. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against a normal {errors_before}. A new release introduced a division-by-zero error in the monthly spend summary, and a feature flag sent shoppers through that code. Argus first tried to roll the release back, but the deployment platform could not be reached. It then switched the feature flag off, and the error rate returned to normal. A draft pull request with a code fix has been proposed and is awaiting review. Until it is merged, turning the flag back on would bring the errors back.

got_lucky: A feature flag gated the faulty path, so the traffic could be turned off without a rollback. Had the code run for all traffic, the unreachable platform would have left no quick mitigation.
The defect is still in production behind the flag. If someone turns the flag back on before the fix is merged, the errors will return.
went_well: Argus fell back to the next candidate within seconds of finding the platform unreachable, and the flag revert was confirmed against the metrics.
The logs clearly showed the exception and its location, and a draft fix pull request was proposed soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: The Investigator ranked the deploy as the leading cause, and the flag reading (C2) as a weaker alternative. The flag revert (C2) was what worked, so the ranking did not match the evidence.
The platform rollback (M1) was unavailable, so the first mitigation attempt did nothing.
The alert came well after the errors began, and shoppers had no account pages in the meantime.

input.root_cause: The revision deployed at {began} changed the spend-summary code in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py so that it raises ZeroDivisionError (line 47) for some accounts. The monthly-spend-feature flag routed account-page traffic through that code. The errors stopped only when the flag was switched off. The defect is still in the deployed code.
